analysis.one_liner: Lets workers and consumers take race discrimination claims to court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on November 20, 2025 and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearing or vote scheduled and all 10 sponsors are Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: Nearly every employment contract today forces workers to resolve disputes through private arbitration instead of court, and many consumer contracts do the same. This bill would change that for one category of claims: if someone alleges discrimination, harassment, or retaliation based on race, color, or national origin, they could choose to go to court with a judge and jury — and join class actions — even if they signed an arbitration agreement. Courts, not arbitrators, would decide whether the law applies. It mirrors a 2022 law that did the same thing for sexual assault and harassment claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, job applicants, and consumers who face race discrimination and currently must take their claims to a private arbitrator chosen under a contract they had little real choice but to sign. Court proceedings are public, appealable, and allow class actions, which matter for lower-dollar discrimination claims that are not worth pursuing alone.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers facing race discrimination

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes predispute arbitration agreements and joint-action (class waiver) clauses unenforceable for race discrimination disputes, at the election of the person claiming discrimination or a class representative.
It covers discrimination, harassment, or retaliation based on race, color, or national origin under federal, Tribal, state, or local law.
A court, not an arbitrator, decides whether the law applies, even if the contract purports to delegate that decision to an arbitrator.
The change applies only to claims that arise after the bill is enacted, so it does not disturb existing cases.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and companies that rely on mandatory arbitration clauses would face public lawsuits, juries, appeals, and possible class actions over race discrimination claims. Arbitration providers and the private arbitrators they supply would lose a category of business. Employers argue these public cases are slower and costlier; workers' advocates argue that is precisely the accountability arbitration avoids.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration is often faster and cheaper than court for an individual worker, and the bill only opens the courthouse door for claims arising after enactment — it does nothing for past cases.

Employers and arbitration's supporters argue that some low-value discrimination claims are more practical to resolve in arbitration, and that removing arbitration for this category could push companies toward pre-dispute mandatory settlement terms or other screening instead.

The bill is one-sided by design: it does not touch arbitration for other discrimination types or contract disputes, so the same contract could send a wage claim to arbitration while a race discrimination claim from the same events goes to court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is access versus speed. Giving people a real choice between a public court and private arbitration addresses a well-documented weakness of arbitration — no jury, no appeal, no class actions, and a private decision-maker chosen under the employer's contract — at the cost of slower, more expensive individual cases for some. The 2022 version of this approach for sexual harassment claims passed with heavy bipartisan support, which suggests the model can be designed to work in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on November 20, 2025, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no vote, and no Republican support yet.

narrative.text: Senator Booker introduced the bill on November 20, 2025 with nine Democratic cosponsors, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day.
The bill's only action since referral is nothing: no committee business, no floor vote, and no further amendments appear in its action history.
All ten senators behind the bill are Democrats; no Republican has joined.
The bill is modeled on title 9 of the U.S. Code, adding a new chapter making race discrimination arbitration clauses unenforceable at the claimant's election.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers with arbitration clauses and arbitration providers — the status quo they operate under has not been disturbed, and the bill has not moved.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led ten Democratic senators on it.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors are Democrats — Booker plus 9 of the Senate's 45 Democrats — and no Republican has cosponsored; the committee it sits in has not acted.

industries.note: Employer-side arbitration agreements and class-action waivers would become unenforceable for race discrimination claims, exposing companies to public trials and collective actions they currently can channel into private arbitration. Their interest in keeping disputes private runs against workers' access to open court proceedings.
Race discrimination cases are a source of fee-generating arbitrations; the bill removes them at the claimant's election. Their business depends on the status quo the bill would unwind.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' employment and civil rights bar
industries.note: Attorneys representing discrimination claimants gain a path to court and class actions that arbitration clauses currently block, which changes which claims are economically viable to bring.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Judiciary Committee with no hearing or markup scheduled and no Republican cosponsors, so its odds of passage in this Congress are low unless it picks up the kind of bipartisan coalition that carried the 2022 sexual harassment version of this approach. For now it functions as a statement bill pending any new action.
